description: Feast days, the Grand Tour, railway seaside trips, holiday camps, package holidays abroad.
content_html:
Holidays Before the Railway

For most people in medieval and early modern England, holidays meant feast days and holy days. The word “holiday” derives from “holy day”. The Church calendar provided around forty such days per year, including Christmas, Easter, Whitsun and Michaelmas. These were not just religious occasions — they were the primary leisure breaks available to ordinary working people, who filled them with sport, dancing, fairs and communal feasting.

Travel for leisure was a privilege of the wealthy. In the eighteenth century, upper-class young men undertook the Grand Tour as a cultural education. The typical route included Paris, the Swiss Alps, and the cities of northern Italy — Venice, Florence and Rome. Young men spent months or years abroad, studying art, architecture and antiquities, and returned with Continental tastes and acquired artworks. It was expensive, time-consuming and available only to the elite.

Key Fact

Thomas Cook organised the first commercially promoted railway excursion in 1841 — a trip from Leicester to Loughborough for a temperance rally. He went on to develop package tours to the seaside and eventually abroad, making leisure travel accessible to the middle classes and, later, the working class.

The Railway and the Seaside

The rapid expansion of the railway network after the 1840s transformed the British holiday. Resorts that had previously been accessible only to wealthy visitors who could travel by coach suddenly became reachable in hours from industrial cities. Blackpool, accessible by rail from Manchester and Preston from the 1840s onwards, grew from a small village into a major resort. Brighton, already fashionable among London’s elite, was transformed when the London–Brighton line opened in 1841, cutting the journey to under two hours.

Seaside resorts invested heavily in attractions: piers, promenades, theatres, bandstands and amusement arcades. The railway brought day-trippers and week-long holidaymakers alike. Blackpool built its famous tower in 1894, modelled on the Eiffel Tower. By the late nineteenth century, the seaside holiday had become a defining feature of working-class leisure culture in industrial Britain.

The Bank Holiday Act of 1871, introduced by Sir John Lubbock, created official public holidays — Easter Monday, Whit Monday, the first Monday in August, and Boxing Day. These were not paid holidays for most workers initially, but they established the principle of regular leisure time. Crucially, they coincided with the growth of cheap rail travel, making day trips and short breaks possible for millions.

Paid holidays came later and unevenly. Some workers had negotiated a week’s paid leave by the early twentieth century, but millions had none. The Holidays with Pay Act of 1938 required employers to give workers at least one week’s paid holiday per year — though war interrupted its full implementation. By the 1950s and 1960s, two weeks of paid annual leave was becoming the norm, fundamentally changing the scale of the British holiday market.

Holiday Camps and National Parks

The 1930s saw the rise of the holiday camp. Billy Butlin opened his first camp at Skegness in 1936, offering an all-inclusive holiday at a fixed price. Holiday camps were designed to give working-class families a full week’s holiday without the worry of organising food, accommodation and entertainment separately. By the early 1950s, Butlin’s camps were hosting around a million visitors a year. The holiday camp model represented a new democratisation of the British holiday.

The National Parks and Access to the Countryside Act of 1949 created the first national parks in England and Wales, designating areas of outstanding natural beauty for public enjoyment. The Peak District became the first national park in 1951. Improved bus and car ownership allowed day-trippers and hikers to reach the countryside in growing numbers through the 1950s and 1960s.

Package holidays to the Mediterranean expanded rapidly during the 1960s. Vladimir Raitz of Horizon Holidays organised the first modern package tour to Corsica in 1950, and the market grew quickly once jet aviation made the journey faster. By the early 1970s, millions of British holidaymakers were flying to Spain, Greece and Portugal each year. Low-cost airlines like Ryanair and easyJet, which expanded during the 1990s, further reduced the cost of foreign travel.

The consequence for British seaside resorts was devastating. Blackpool, Skegness, Margate and other traditional resorts faced declining visitor numbers from the 1970s onwards. They struggled to compete with guaranteed sunshine, cheap wine and modern hotels abroad. Some invested in new attractions — Blackpool added a major indoor entertainment complex. Others declined sharply, with high unemployment and derelict seafronts becoming a visible social problem by the 1980s.

Key Fact

The growth of cheap air travel and Mediterranean package holidays from the 1960s fundamentally changed British holiday patterns. Millions chose Spain and Greece over Blackpool and Scarborough. British seaside resorts experienced serious decline: by the 1970s many were losing visitors rapidly to foreign destinations.

Change and Continuity

Tracing holiday patterns from c.500 to the present reveals a clear pattern of gradual widening access. Medieval feast days were universally available but brief; the Grand Tour was exclusive and long. The railway opened the seaside to the urban working class; bank holidays and paid leave formalised leisure time; holiday camps democratised the week-away holiday; package holidays exported British leisure culture to the Mediterranean. Technology — the steam locomotive, the jet aircraft, the budget airline — was the decisive driver of each shift. Throughout, class shaped both what was possible and where people went.
exam_tip_html: On a thematic change essay about holidays, always cover all three eras: medieval (feast days, Grand Tour), early modern (railways, Bank Holiday Act), and modern (holiday camps, package holidays). Don’t ignore continuity: the link between wealth and holiday quality persisted from the Grand Tour to the package-holiday era, when richer families still chose exclusive destinations. Make sure your conclusion states clearly how much things changed overall — a strong essay has a substantiated judgement, not just a list of changes.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Medieval holy days gave ordinary people brief leisure breaks; the eighteenth-century Grand Tour gave wealthy young men extended cultural travel — both patterns show class shaping holiday access.
  • The railway after the 1840s, the Bank Holiday Act 1871 and the Holidays with Pay Act 1938 progressively widened access to leisure travel, culminating in the holiday camp model of the 1930s.
  • Package holidays from the 1960s transformed British leisure abroad while devastating domestic seaside resorts; cheap airlines from the 1990s deepened this shift.

practice_questions.text: Describe one feature of feast days as a form of holiday in medieval England.
practice_questions.marks: One feature with detail: e.g. feast days were provided by the Church calendar, giving ordinary workers around forty leisure days per year / they were occasions for sport, dancing and communal feasting, not only religious observance. [2 marks]

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of the impact of the railway on British holidays after the 1840s.
practice_questions.marks: Two features each developed: e.g. the railway made seaside resorts accessible to industrial cities — Blackpool became reachable from Manchester in hours (feature + detail); resorts invested in piers, towers and entertainment to meet the new demand from day-trippers (feature + detail). [4 marks: 2 per feature]

practice_questions.text: Explain one reason why British seaside resorts went into decline after the 1960s.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Developed causal explanation linking the growth of cheap air travel and Mediterranean package holidays (guaranteed sunshine, modern hotels, cheap wine) to falling visitor numbers at resorts like Blackpool. Specific evidence (e.g. Ryanair, easyJet, 1970s decline). Secure: Clear cause with supporting detail. Developing: Simple reason. Emerging: Basic point. [6 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain one consequence of the Holidays with Pay Act of 1938 for British workers.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Developed consequence explaining how guaranteed paid leave expanded the holiday market, enabled more workers to take week-long seaside holidays, and supported the growth of the holiday camp industry. Evidence-based. Secure: Clear consequence with supporting detail. Developing: Simple consequence. Emerging: Basic point. [6 marks]

practice_questions.text: How significant was technology in changing British holiday patterns between 1840 and the present day?
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Analyses technological significance at the time (railway → seaside) AND over time (jet aircraft → package holidays → budget airlines). Weighs technology against other factors (legislation, rising wages). Secure: Clear analysis of technology’s role with named examples. Developing: Some points, limited range. Emerging: Basic statement. [8 marks]

practice_questions.text: 'The most important change in British holiday patterns was the move from domestic to foreign holidays after 1960.' How far do you agree? Use evidence from across the full period c.500 to the present.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Substantiated judgement. Agrees with strong evidence (package holidays, cheap airlines, decline of British resorts). Challenges by noting earlier turning points were also transformative (railway/seaside democratisation; Holidays with Pay Act enabling mass holidays). Traces all three eras. Overall conclusion weighs relative importance. Secure: Addresses both sides with evidence across two or more eras. Developing: Some argument, limited range. Emerging: Simple agree/disagree. [16 marks]

knowledge_checks.q: What did the Bank Holiday Act of 1871 introduce?
options: Paid annual leave for all workers
Four official public holidays in England
The right to two weeks' holiday per year

knowledge_checks.q: Who opened the first Butlin's holiday camp, at Skegness, in 1936?
The _____ Act of 1938 required employers to provide workers with at least one week of paid holiday per year.
Thomas Cook organised the first commercially promoted railway excursion in _____, from Leicester to Loughborough.
Match each term to its correct description:
right: Church-provided leisure breaks available to ordinary medieval people
Extended European cultural tour taken by wealthy young Englishmen in the eighteenth century
Flights, accommodation and transfers sold together, making foreign holidays affordable

flashcard_questions.q: What were 'feast days and holy days' in medieval England?
flashcard_questions.a: Church-calendar leisure breaks providing sport, dancing and communal feasting — the main holidays for ordinary people.
An extended European tour taken by wealthy young Englishmen as a cultural education in the eighteenth century.

flashcard_questions.q: When did Thomas Cook organise his first railway excursion?
How many official public holidays did the Bank Holiday Act of 1871 create in England, Wales and Ireland?
flashcard_questions.a: Four official public holidays, including Easter Monday, Whit Monday, the first Monday in August, and Boxing Day.

flashcard_questions.q: When did the Holidays with Pay Act come into force, and what did it require?
flashcard_questions.a: 1938; employers had to give workers at least one week's paid holiday per year.

flashcard_questions.q: Who opened the first Butlin's holiday camp, and where?

flashcard_questions.a: Large organised resorts that provided a complete holiday experience at a fixed price, removing the need to arrange accommodation, food and entertainment separately.

flashcard_questions.q: What happened to British seaside resorts from the 1970s onwards?
flashcard_questions.a: Visitor numbers declined sharply as package holidays abroad became cheap and popular.
A holiday where flights, accommodation and transfers are bundled together at one price, making foreign travel affordable for ordinary families.

flashcard_questions.q: The Peak District became Britain's first national park in what year?
Which airlines drove the expansion of cheap foreign travel in the 1990s?
What was the single biggest driver of change in British holiday patterns across the whole period c.500 to present?
flashcard_questions.a: Technology — the railway, then the jet aircraft, then the budget airline.

glossary_terms.definition: Days set aside by the Church for religious observance and celebration, which also served as the main leisure breaks for ordinary people.
An extended tour of European cultural sites, particularly in France and Italy, taken by wealthy young Englishmen as an educational rite of passage in the eighteenth century.
Legislation passed in 1871 that created four official public holidays in England, Wales and Ireland, and five in Scotland.
Large organised holiday resorts providing accommodation, meals and entertainment all at one price, pioneered by Billy Butlin in the 1930s.
A holiday where flights, accommodation and transfers are sold together at one price, making foreign travel affordable for working-class and middle-class Britons.
